query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under service-relevant loading conditions (such as high strain rates or low temperatures), a homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy develops localized nanoscale brittle clusters through a strain-induced ordering transition, which degrade toughness by serving as internal crack initiation sites. This embrittlement mechanism in the HEA is mechanistically distinct from the conventional grain-boundary segregation expected in traditional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy without pre-existing brittle clusters or grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject the high-entropy alloy and a conventional alloy (for controlled comparison) to identical mechanical loading conditions (e.g., high strain rate or cryogenic temperature tests) designed to activate ordering transitions without triggering rapid grain growth.
generation.conditions: Service-like loading conditions (high strain rate or low temperature) that provide sufficient energy to activate local ordering in the HEA without inducing conventional grain-boundary segregation or extensive thermal coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale brittle clusters (ordered regions) that form within the grain interiors of the HEA.
generation.mechanism: The applied mechanical load causes local compositional fluctuations in the HEA, triggering a strain-induced ordering transition that leads to the nucleation of nanoscale brittle clusters. These clusters serve as stress concentrators and internal crack initiation sites, reducing overall material toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: After loading, the HEA is expected to exhibit dispersed nanoscale brittle clusters within the grain interiors and a measurable decrease in fracture toughness relative to its initial state. In contrast, the conventional alloy should show toughness degradation mainly associated with grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitates.
generation.baseline: The alloy’s initial condition is a uniformly single-phase HEA with homogeneous toughness and no localized brittle clusters.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under controlled mechanical loading conditions (e.g., high strain rate or low-temperature tests) that maintain the alloy in the single-phase region. Deviations from these conditions (such as prolonged thermal exposure causing grain growth) may invoke alternative degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: While the formation of nanoscale brittle clusters is predicted, there is some uncertainty regarding the precise load thresholds and whether minor alternative mechanisms may also contribute to the observed embrittlement in the HEA.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of high-entropy alloy samples and one set of conventional alloy samples with similar baseline toughness. Subject both sets to identical controlled mechanical loading conditions (e.g., high strain rate tensile tests at cryogenic temperatures). Post-deformation, conduct microstructural analysis with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to detect the presence or absence of nanoscale brittle clusters inside the grain interiors in the HEA versus grain-boundary segregation in the conventional alloy. Additionally, evaluate changes in fracture toughness using standardized mechanical tests pre- and post-loading.
measurements: TEM imaging to detect in-grain nanoscale clusters
APT for chemical mapping and confirmation of local ordering
Analysis of grain boundaries for signs of segregation or intermetallic formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not exhibit any in-grain nanoscale brittle clusters and if the drop in fracture toughness correlates primarily with grain-boundary segregation, similarly to the conventional alloy, then the hypothesis—that a strain-induced, in-grain ordering transition causes embrittlement—is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), when exposed to specific service loads (such as high strain rates or low temperatures), local compositional fluctuations under load promote a strain‐induced ordering transition within the grains, leading to the nucleation of nanoscale brittle clusters. These clusters, rather than grain-boundary phenomena, serve as internal crack initiation sites that degrade toughness.
drafts.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure and no pre-existing brittle precipitates or segregated phases.
drafts.intervention: Subject the HEA and a conventional alloy (used for controlled comparison) to matched mechanical loading conditions (e.g., high strain rate deformation or cryogenic temperatures) that are known to activate ordering processes.
drafts.conditions: Testing under service-like conditions where the alloy is loaded at high strain rates or low temperatures, ensuring that the activation energy for local ordering is reached without triggering rapid grain coarsening or conventional intermetallic formation at grain boundaries.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale brittle clusters or ordered regions that emerge within the grain interiors (distinct from grain-boundary segregation or precipitates) as a response to the imposed deformation.
drafts.mechanism: The applied mechanical load drives localized compositional inhomogeneities within the HEA matrix, triggering a thermodynamically favorable ordering transition and phase separation on a nanoscale. This results in the formation of brittle clusters that act as stress concentrators, reducing the overall toughness of the material by promoting crack initiation and propagation from the matrix rather than from the grain boundaries.
drafts.predicted_outcome: After loading, the HEA is predicted to show evidence of dispersed nanoscale brittle clusters in the grain interiors together with a measurable drop in fracture toughness relative to its initial state. In contrast, the conventional alloy should primarily show toughness degradation associated with grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation.
drafts.baseline: The initial condition is a homogeneous, single-phase HEA with uniform toughness and without localized brittle clusters.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under controlled loading regimes (high strain rate or low-temperature tests) where the alloy composition remains in the single-phase region; deviations from these conditions (such as extensive thermal exposure that might induce grain growth) may trigger alternative degradation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of high-entropy alloy samples and one set of conventional alloy samples with comparable baseline toughness. Subject both sets to identical controlled mechanical loading conditions (for example, high strain rate tensile tests conducted at cryogenic temperatures). After loading, use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to analyze the microstructure for evidence of localized, nanoscale brittle clusters within the grain interiors versus grain-boundary segregation. Additionally, measure fracture toughness using standardized tests before and after loading.
measurements: TEM imaging to detect nanocluster formation inside grains
APT for chemical mapping to confirm local ordering
Fracture toughness measurements to quantify degradation
Grain-boundary analysis to check for conventional segregation phenomena
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples do not exhibit any evidence of in-grain nanoscale brittle clustering or if the observed toughness degradation correlates solely with grain-boundary segregation similarly to the conventional alloy, then the hypothesis (that a strain-induced, in-grain ordering transition causes embrittlement) is falsified.
